claims.text: The identity of X governs oxide-scale stability by affecting oxidation kinetics and oxide-phase formation in CrFeCoNiX alloys.
Al has a high affinity for oxygen in the stated CrFeCoNiAl system.
Al promotes formation of a slow-growing, adherent Al2O3 scale on CrFeCoNiAl.
The proposed Al2O3 scale limits oxygen penetration.
The proposed Al2O3 scale minimizes thermal-expansion mismatch with the alloy substrate.
Mn undergoes relatively rapid outward diffusion during oxidation of CrFeCoNiMn.
Si undergoes relatively rapid outward diffusion during oxidation of CrFeCoNiSi.
Mn- and Si-containing oxides have higher volumetric strains that produce noncoherent scales.
High volumetric strain in the Mn- and Si-containing scales causes cracking and spallation.
Exposure at approximately 900–1100 °C in an oxygen-containing atmosphere produces layered oxides in CrFeCoNiMn, including Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides.
Mn mobility and oxide formation can deplete Mn from the alloy, produce pores, and accelerate oxide growth.
Al oxidation produces a dense, thin Al2O3 layer with lower oxygen diffusivity.
Mn- or Si-containing scales develop stress from oxide volume changes and thermal-expansion anisotropy.
CrFeCoNiAl will form a more coherent, slower-growing, and more crack-resistant oxide scale than CrFeCoNiMn or CrFeCoNiSi under otherwise identical high-temperature exposure.
CrFeCoNiMn and CrFeCoNiSi oxide scales will tend to crack and spall during prolonged exposure.
The proposed comparative mechanism applies not only to oxidizing atmospheres but also to unspecified corrosive atmospheres above 900 °C.
Processing history and small compositional deviations can alter diffusion rates, thermal-expansion mismatch, and scale-stress evolution.
The atomic-scale oxidation mechanisms and stability of surface oxides in these multi-principal-element alloys remain incompletely understood.
